Planning, he said, is a tool that begins with a thought and ends in an action, such as a list or a phone call, whereas worry simply goes round and round without ever arriving anywhere. The test of a useful thought, he said, is whether it leads to a step that you can actually take.

Yusuf gave her a simple test to apply to every anxious thought, which was to ask whether there was a step that she could take. If there was, she should write it down, in plain words, and then do it at the first opportunity, and if there was not, she should recognise the thought as weather and let it blow through. Elise tried the test on Thursday's staff meeting and found that three worries became two phone calls and one forgotten spreadsheet.

Elise admitted that, deep down, she believed worrying protected her, as if the disaster might notice her vigilance and go away. Yusuf opened an enormous umbrella under a perfectly clear sky and observed that no amount of worry had ever stopped a single raindrop, whereas an umbrella, calmly packed, had saved him many times. Worry stands outside in the weather, he said, and planning simply carries the umbrella.

Elise decided to put the idea to work, so she took a pad and a pencil to the bench and planned the following week's shifts in the open air. She gave the task fifteen minutes of her full attention, with no phone and no wandering, and the rota fell into place with surprising ease. It had taken her an hour of tangled, anxious effort the week before, and she wondered how much of her working life had been spent on worry disguised as planning.

When the plan was complete, Elise closed the notebook with a decisive click and told herself, almost aloud, that the planning was over. A good plan, she reflected, has an ending, and the ending is permission to stop thinking about it until the plan needs her again. The relief was remarkable, like putting down a heavy shopping bag after a very long walk.

While she was pulling weeds from between the bean plants, Elise caught her mind rehearsing a difficult conversation with her manager, complete with gestures. She whispered the single word rehearsing, rather as one might say good morning to a neighbour, and returned her attention to the dandelion root in her hand. It took less than a second, and it felt like stepping off a moving train onto a still platform.

On Saturday morning, a row of bright green shoots had pushed through the soil along the string line, each one curled like a question mark. Yusuf crouched beside them and pointed out that nothing in the garden had grown in the future or the past, because every plant grew in the present, a tiny amount at a time. Elise knelt to look more closely, and for several minutes she thought about absolutely nothing except beans.

Over a cup of tea in the shed, Yusuf made a deceptively simple observation: everything Elise had ever accomplished or enjoyed had occurred in a present moment, and everything she would ever do would occur in one as well. Even a memory, he pointed out, is something one has now, and even a plan is merely a thought that somebody is thinking at this very instant. Life never actually visits the past or the future, he said, because it keeps turning up exactly where we stand.

Elise objected that her past had surely made her who she was, and that it could not be dismissed as something that did not exist. Yusuf agreed at once, and added that the past was indeed powerful, but that it only ever reached her in the form of a memory or a habit, which arrived in the present. It shaped her, he said, the way a river shapes a bank, by acting on it today.

Yusuf set two cups on the table, one empty and one full, and announced that the empty cup held yesterday's tea and the full one tomorrow's. Elise, playing along, tried to drink from each in turn, and discovered that the first contained nothing and the second could not be reached. Only the cup in her hand, which was at that very moment warm and fragrant, could actually be tasted.

Yusuf's first exercise was disarmingly simple: Elise was to kneel beside him, close her eyes, push her hands into the cool soil, and notice what she felt. There was nothing to achieve, he assured her, and no right answer waiting at the end, only whatever happened to be there. She felt faintly self-conscious, like a woman about to be photographed, and then she began to feel the earth.

The earth was cool and damp and slightly rough, and as her fingers sank in she became aware of tiny stones, of threads of root, and of crumbs slipping between her knuckles like warm sand in an hourglass. She had handled soil as a child, yet she had never actually felt it. It seemed astonishing that something so ordinary, so ignored, could hold such a wealth of detail.

Deeper down, her fingertips found a layer of unexpected warmth, where the morning sun had been quietly working, and she let her hands rest there like cats on a radiator. Then something soft and slippery wriggled across her knuckle, and she shrieked and jerked backwards, to Yusuf's delight. The worm, he said, was only a colleague, and it had every right to be there.

For several seconds, while she attended to nothing but the sensation in her fingers, Elise's tireless thoughts fell quiet. It was not a miracle, and no angels appeared above the beans, but it was the first real rest her mind had had for weeks. She opened her eyes, and the garden looked slightly brighter, as though someone had washed the window.

In the middle of her second try, a thought suddenly burst in: had she locked the car? Yusuf, who seemed able to read her face, said that thoughts would always arrive uninvited, like neighbours, and that the practice was only to greet them and return to her hands. She did so, a little amazed that the car, which had been the most urgent thing in the world a moment earlier, now seemed distant and small.

To wash her muddy hands, Elise dipped them into the rain barrel and gasped at the sudden cold, which ran up her wrists like a small electric current. She watched the clouds of soil dissolve and the light dance across the surface, and she felt every ripple with a clarity that startled her. This, Yusuf said quietly, was the whole of the practice, and it had been waiting for her under the lid of an ordinary barrel.

Before she left, Yusuf reminded Elise that she did not need a garden or an hour of silence to practise, only a single chosen moment each day. It could be the first sip of tea, or the feeling of the door handle, or the moment when the train doors opened, provided that she gave it her whole attention. Elise chose the first sip of tea, and was surprised to find, on Monday, that she looked forward to it.

Yusuf taught her a quick trick for noisy moments, which is to name five things that she could see, four that she could touch, three that she could hear, two that she could smell and one that she could taste. By the time she had reached the sparrow's chatter and the faint scent of tomato leaves, her racing thoughts had slowed down to the speed of her senses. The senses, he said, always live in the present, and so they make a handy door back into it.

Yusuf asked her to begin with her eyes, and Elise looked properly at the garden for the first time. She picked out a blue bucket, a robin on the fence, a ladder leaning on the shed, a snail on a wall and a bright patch of sun on the path. It struck her that she had passed these things earlier without seeing a single one, and naming them seemed to bring each into focus, as if the garden had been blurred all along.

Next came touch, and Elise went around the garden like a visitor in a museum who is allowed to handle the exhibits. She laid her palm against the sun-warmed bench, the rough apple bark, the cool blade of the trowel and, finally, the soft cotton of her own sleeve. Each surface had its own temperature and its own character, and she had never thought of her sleeve as having a character at all; the world, it seemed, was full of textures that she had been too busy to read.

With her eyes closed, Elise let the garden's sounds arrive one by one, like guests waiting politely outside. First came the busy chatter of a sparrow, then the distant sigh of a bus pulling away from a stop, and, beneath both, the soft rustle of the wind in the bean leaves. She had always supposed that the city was simply noisy, but now she could hear that it was layered, like a piece of music with a quiet bass note, and that such richness had been available all along.

For smell, Elise crushed a tomato leaf between her fingers and breathed in its sharp, green, almost peppery scent, and then she bent to the damp earth and caught its deeper perfume. For taste, Yusuf pressed a mug of mint tea into her hands, and she sipped it slowly, noticing the heat, the sweetness and the cool afterglow of the mint. When the exercise was over, her mind felt quiet and wide, like a room after the furniture has been carried out into the sun.

Yusuf explained why the trick worked, and the explanation was pleasantly simple: the senses have no access to yesterday or tomorrow, and they report only on what is happening here and now. Each time Elise turned her attention to what she could see or hear, she was therefore stepping through a door into the present, however far her thoughts had travelled. The door was always there, he said, and it never needed to be unlocked.

Rosa, a sixteen-year-old who came to the garden on Saturdays to earn volunteering hours for school, pulled off her headphones and asked, with a sceptical eyebrow, whether all of this was simply paying attention. Yusuf beamed as though she had solved a famous riddle and replied that it was exactly that, and that its simplicity was precisely what made it difficult. Rosa shrugged, put her headphones back on, and then, to Elise's amusement, turned the music down.

On Monday morning, the platform was crowded, the train was late, and Elise could feel her shoulders creeping towards her ears. Instead of reaching for her phone, she quietly named five things that she could see: a yellow line, a pair of red shoes, a pigeon on a girder, a poster for a musical, and a man doing a crossword. The tension did not vanish, but it loosened its grip, and when the train arrived she boarded it feeling oddly lighter.

After a tense telephone call about a ward with no night staff, Elise stood in the hospital corridor with her heart hammering against her ribs. She planted her feet flat on the floor and named what she could see, a green line along the wall, a clock, a poster about hand washing and a squeaking trolley, until her pulse had slowed enough to think. The problem was exactly as large as it had been a minute earlier, but she was a good deal better equipped to meet it.

That evening, Elise thought carefully about what the practice had actually done, and she concluded that it had not removed a single problem from her life. What it had given her was a place to stand, a small and stable patch of ground from which to look at the problems and decide what to do. It was, she reflected, rather like Yusuf's smallest circle, and it was always available, provided that she remembered to step into it.

The breath, Yusuf said, is the most faithful companion any person has, because it is always with you and it always happens now. It has never once missed an appointment, he added, and it does not need a charger, a password or a subscription. Elise, who had felt tracked and measured by devices all week, found this remarkably consoling and a little funny.

Yusuf asked her to take three slow breaths and to count them, feeling the air enter, rest and leave. Elise was surprised by how much longer three breaths took than she had imagined, and by how often her attention slipped away between one and two. The numbers, she discovered, were considerably harder to keep hold of than a long and complicated shopping list.

Slow breathing often helps the body to settle, and, to her quiet astonishment, hers settled a little too. Her shoulders drifted down from the neighbourhood of her ears, her jaw unclenched, and a tightness that she had carried for so long that it felt like part of her posture began to ease. It was not dramatic, but it was perfectly real, and it had cost her nothing but a few minutes of her Saturday.

Elise lost count at the second breath and announced, with some embarrassment, that she had already failed the exercise. Yusuf said that there was nothing to fail, and that the correct response was simply to begin again at one, with no medals for the person who arrived at ten first. Beginning again, he added with a twinkle in his eye, was the only real skill involved in the whole business.

Yusuf had Elise lie on the grass and watch the clouds drift across the sky, and he suggested that her thoughts were rather like weather passing through it. A thought, he said, is an event in the mind and not a fact about the world, even when it arrives with a very serious face. Some are white and harmless, some are grey and heavy, but all of them move on if they are not chased.

Elise took a pencil and wrote down the thought that had been following her all week, which was that she would never get through her work. Seeing it on the page, in her own cramped handwriting, she realised that it was a cloud and not a forecast, and that she had been treating it as the truth for days. The sentence looked much smaller on paper than it had felt inside her head.

A heavier thought rolled in, telling Elise that she was hopeless at this and should stop wasting her Saturdays, and for a moment it blotted out everything else. Yusuf looked up at an actual storm cloud overhead and remarked, quite cheerfully, that it was a magnificent one, but that no storm in the history of the sky had ever stayed forever. The thought grumbled for several minutes, and then, like the cloud, it drifted off to bother somebody else.

Yusuf taught her a gentle technique, which was to give each thought a quiet label as it passed, such as planning, remembering or worrying. A named thought, he explained, was like a cloud in a field guide, easier to watch and harder to be swept away by. Elise noticed that by naming her thoughts she stood slightly apart from them, in the way that a person on a riverbank stands apart from the water.

Behind each cloud, Yusuf pointed out, the sky was still quietly there, and it had never once been disturbed by the weather that crossed it. Elise looked up through the branches and felt, for a brief and slightly dizzying moment, that some part of her was like that sky, watching her thoughts pass without being any of them. She did not know what to call it, and for once she did not feel that she needed to.

As homework, Yusuf suggested three slow breaths at every pedestrian crossing, a task that Elise treated with the seriousness of a person cramming for an examination. By Monday afternoon she had discovered that her day contained dozens of these tiny pauses, at crossings, in lifts and beside printers, each one a free opportunity that she had previously spent on her phone. The red light, once an irritation, had become one of the more pleasant moments of her morning.

On Monday, Elise resolved to try one full minute of stillness at her desk, between two meetings and before the next wave of messages. She closed her eyes, sat up straight, and took a slow breath, but the screen of glowing schedules seemed to follow her into the dark behind her eyelids. It was a bold little experiment, and she had no idea at all whether it would work or end in disaster.

Within five seconds the thoughts had rushed back in, loud and urgent, led by a spreadsheet that would not balance and a nurse who had called in sick. Then a telephone rang on the next desk, and at forty seconds Elise gave up, opened her eyes, and glared at the clock as if it had been cheating. It was, she thought, quite possibly the longest minute of her entire working life, and she had not even reached a minute.

On Saturday, Elise confessed that her minute at the desk had been a complete failure, and she described the spreadsheet, the telephone and the forty seconds with some bitterness. Yusuf listened with every sign of delight and then said that she had not failed at all, because wandering was perfectly normal and the only real requirement was to notice it. By that measure, he said, she had succeeded several times before the telephone rang.

Yusuf hoisted a full watering can by the handle, held it out at arm's length, and compared the practice to a repetition at the gym. Each time Elise noticed that her mind had wandered and brought it back, he said, she was lifting the weight once more, and attention, like any muscle, grew stronger with use. The wandering was therefore not an obstacle to the training but the very thing that made the training possible.

Elise sat for three minutes with her hand resting on her knee, counting on her fingers each time her mind wandered and each time she brought it back. She reached seventeen returns, a number that would have depressed her a week earlier, and Yusuf congratulated her on a magnificent workout. Seventeen repetitions, he said with great gravity, was a serious training session by anybody's standards, and he suggested that she reward herself with a biscuit.

Elise asked whether the wandering ever stopped, and Yusuf laughed so heartily that he had to lean on his spade. After many years of practice, he said, his mind still wandered all the time, and only last week he had dug up an entire bed of onions by mistake while thinking about a cheese sandwich. The difference, he explained, was not that he wandered less but that he returned a little sooner and with far less embarrassment.

At the hospital one evening, Priya Nair, a night nurse with shadows under her eyes, paused beside the drinks machine and remarked that Elise seemed unusually calm. Elise laughed, surprised to be noticed, and replied that it was a long story involving beans, an old gardener and a very small circle of earth. Priya raised an eyebrow, but she did not walk away, and it was clear that she wanted to hear the whole story.

Priya confessed that after a night shift her body was exhausted but her mind kept racing around the ward, checking charts and replaying decisions long after she had gone to bed. Elise listened without offering advice, and, as she described the garden, she watched something in Priya's face soften. Priya said with a tired smile that she could use a garden herself, and Elise heard herself say that she would be very welcome.

Elise decided to attach the practice to something that she already did every day, since a habit with no hook has a way of falling off the wall. Each time she sat down at her desk, she would feel both feet resting on the floor and take one slow breath before touching the keyboard. It was a tiny ritual, but, repeated a dozen times a day, it began to feel like a series of small homecomings.

On Saturday, the first radishes were ready, and Yusuf let Elise pull one from the earth with her own hand. It came up round and glossy, with a wisp of root trailing behind it, and she held it up like a trophy and laughed out loud at her own pleasure. She had planted that row weeks earlier, half asleep and half absent, and it had grown anyway, without any help from her worrying.

Yusuf led her to the carrot bed, where a small wooden sign marked the spot and nothing whatever was visible above the soil. Carrots, he said, take their time and cannot be hurried by anyone, and the weeks before they sprout are among the most important of their lives. Elise looked at the smooth brown earth and tried to imagine something orange working away in the dark.

After three days of anxious visits, Elise could not resist the urge to scratch up one seed and see how it was getting on. Yusuf caught her wrist, gently but firmly, and explained that digging up a seed to inspect its progress was the surest way to slow it down. A carrot cannot be pulled out of the ground into being, he said, and a person cannot be pulled into patience either.

At work, a shortage of weekend staff landed on Elise's desk, and she wanted to have it solved by the end of the day. The solution, however, depended on replies from three managers, two agencies and one nurse on holiday, and no amount of impatience on her part could speed up any of them. She sent her messages with care, took a slow breath, and thought of the carrots.

The gardener's work, Yusuf told her, falls into two parts: he prepares the bed, sows the seed and waters it, and then the soil does its part in its own time. Elise decided to apply the same rule at the hospital, doing everything that lay in her power and then resting from it without gnawing at the rest. It was a surprisingly relaxing way to arrange her sense of responsibility, and it did not make her any less careful at all.

That evening, Elise decided to cook dinner in the way that she was beginning to do most things, which was with one thing at a time and no podcast. She chopped the vegetables slowly on the wooden board, watching the knife and the pale curve of each slice instead of staring into the middle distance. The kitchen, which was usually a place of rushing and clattering, felt almost spacious and calm.

As she cut into the onion, Elise noticed the dry whisper of the skin, the steady knock of the knife and the sharp steam that stung her eyes. Her tears ran down, and she laughed at herself, because she had cooked onions hundreds of times and had never really met one before. When the pieces finally hit the hot pan, the sizzle was so loud and so cheerful that it startled her into laughing again.

While the sauce simmered, Elise's mind drifted off towards her inbox, and she felt the familiar pull of the unanswered message. She noticed, smiled, and returned to the wooden spoon, to the steam and to the first taste of the sauce, in which she distinguished the garlic from the tomato for what seemed like the first time. Her cooking, she thought, had apparently been delicious for years, and she had missed it.

She carried her plate to the table, left the television dark, and ate slowly, tasting each mouthful in turn and putting her fork down between bites. The meal lasted twenty minutes instead of the usual eight, and when she had finished she felt pleasantly full in a way that gulping in front of a screen had never produced. It was the same sauce, the same pasta and the same woman, but the experience had been transformed.

Yusuf told her that when we try to do two things at once, we are usually switching rapidly between them, and each one suffers a little. Elise recalled her own working days, in which she answered messages during meetings and joined calls while checking schedules, and she realised how many small mistakes had come from that constant switching. A single task, done fully, seemed less a luxury than a form of efficiency.

One Saturday, a row of fine green threads appeared along the line where the sign stood, so delicate that they looked as though they had been drawn with a fine pen. Elise knelt to examine them, enchanted, and found that she was grinning like a child at a magic show. Nothing had been done to hurry them, she realised, and perhaps that was exactly why they looked so beautiful.

One evening, Elise decided to make a small tally mark on a sticky note every time she picked up her phone, and she found the results alarming. By nine o'clock the note was covered in neat little fences of five, and she had to turn it over to find more room. She had not been doing anything important with the phone, which was the worst part, because she had simply been reaching for it.

Elise began to notice that every buzz and flash of the screen pulled her attention away from whatever she was doing, in the way that a child tugs at a sleeve. Reading a single page of her novel took ten minutes, because she was interrupted so often that she had to keep returning to the top of it. Her attention, she realised, had been chopped into such small pieces that she was no longer sure that she owned the whole.

At dinner, Elise placed her phone in the kitchen drawer and closed it with a small, ceremonial thump. For the first ten minutes she felt twitchy and exposed, like a person who has left the house without her keys, and twice her hand moved on its own towards the place where the phone should have been. She kept her hand in her lap and waited for the feeling to pass, which, to her relief, it eventually did.

After a week, the twitchy feeling was gone, and in the space it left behind Elise found a number of things she had not known were there. She heard the tick of the kitchen clock, noticed that the toast tasted slightly of butter and smoke, and watched the evening light slide slowly across the table. The drawer had not taken anything from her, she thought, and had in fact returned several hours of her life.

On Sunday, Elise rang the bell at her sister's small, cheerful house with a bunch of flowers in one hand and a gift for Lily in the other. She had left her phone in the pocket of her coat in the hall, a small act of courage that made her feel unexpectedly light. The door flew open, and a six-year-old in a paper crown hurled herself at her aunt's knees.

Over coffee at the kitchen table, Elise apologised in person for the cancelled birthday dinner, which she found was much harder than doing it by message. Nora waved the apology away with a kind smile, and then, almost casually, admitted that she had been exhausted and anxious for weeks about her new job. It was the first time in a long while that either sister had said something real.

Elise listened to her sister with her whole attention, which she realised was something she had not done for years. She did not plan her reply while Nora was still speaking, nor reach for the usual tidy advice, and when the urge to fix things arose she noticed it and let it pass. She simply looked at her sister's tired face and heard, perhaps for the first time in years, everything that she was saying.

Nora's eyes filled, and she wiped them with a napkin and laughed at herself, and then she said that it was lovely to have her sister actually present for once. The words stung a little, because they were true, but they also warmed her more than anything had in weeks, and Elise squeezed her hand without saying anything at all. There was nothing that she could usefully add, and for once she did not try to add anything at all.

After lunch, Lily proudly presented her aunt with a drawing of a purple dragon, with green wings and a surprising number of teeth. Elise knelt on the carpet and examined every part of it, asked thoughtful questions about the tail and the smoke, and listened to the long and entirely invented history of the dragon's life. Lily glowed like a lamp, and it dawned on Elise that attention was the best present she had ever given a child.

Elise walked home through the long gold light of the summer evening with the purple dragon rolled up under her arm. She realised, somewhere between the corner shop and her front door, that it had been the best Sunday she had spent in a year, and that nothing extraordinary had happened to make it so. She had simply been present for all of it, and that, it seemed, was the extraordinary thing.

Yusuf pressed a tangerine into her hand and asked her to look at it before she did anything else. She turned it over, felt the dimpled skin and peeled it slowly, and a bright, sharp scent rose into the warm air of the garden. Her fingers shone with oil, and, for the first time in years, she felt properly introduced to a piece of fruit.

Elise held a single segment up to the light and examined it as though she had been given a jewel to value. She saw the fine white threads that clung to it, the translucent skin shining like silk, and the tiny packed bubbles of juice that glowed from within. It was beautiful in a quiet way, and it had been sitting in fruit bowls all her life, ignored.

She placed the segment on her tongue and, for once, did not hurry to swallow it. The flavour unfolded in stages, sweet at first, then sharply sour, then sweet again, with a faint bitterness at the edge that made the rest taste brighter. One small piece lasted for a full minute, and she realised that she had been eating most of her life without actually tasting.

Elise knew that she could not spend an hour on every meal, so she chose one a day to eat with her full attention, and she picked breakfast. She sat at the counter with her toast and tea, looked out at the street and tasted each mouthful, and within a week it had become the calmest quarter of an hour of her working day. It was a small island, but it was hers, and it floated above the flood of the morning.

Yusuf proposed a walk, and then proceeded to walk so slowly that Elise had to hold herself back from overtaking him. He asked her to feel the heel touching the gravel, then the roll of the foot, then the toes pushing off, and to notice the air on her face and the warmth of the sun on her shoulders. Walking, he said, was not a way of getting somewhere but a way of being somewhere, one step at a time.

On the walk to work the next morning, Elise felt each foot touch the pavement and looked up at the leaves, which cast a restless pattern of green and gold across her path. By the time she reached the hospital door, she did not feel that she had been merely transported there, like a parcel, but that she had actually travelled and arrived. It was an odd distinction, and she was surprised by how much it mattered.

Elise noticed that she habitually walked as though pursued, with her shoulders hunched and her eyes fixed on a distant doorway. She decided to slow down by about a fifth for a week, and she timed the experiment out of curiosity, expecting a disaster. She arrived at the hospital only two minutes later than before, and considerably less out of breath.

At the corner shop, the queue snaked towards a single open till, and the man at its head seemed to be paying in small coins. Elise felt irritation rise in her chest like heat, and she noticed her foot tapping and her jaw tightening and her mind composing a complaint. For a moment she was entirely carried away by it, and then she remembered where she was.

She took three slow breaths, felt her feet flat on the tiles, and let her gaze move gently round the shop instead of fixing on the till. The man at the front, she now saw, was elderly and was holding a single tin of soup, counting out his coins with a care that had nothing to do with slowness and everything to do with pride. Her irritation dissolved like sugar in tea, and she was startled by how quickly and completely it went.

By the time she reached the till, Elise was almost sorry that the queue was over, and she smiled at the old man as he shuffled out into the sun. Every queue, she decided, was a free bench set down in the middle of a busy day, and she had been wasting hundreds of them. Waiting, she thought, was not lost time at all, but an unexpected gift wrapped in irritation.

Before an important performance review with her manager, Elise felt her stomach twist into a tight knot, and she was about to ignore it as usual. Instead, remembering Yusuf, she took a yellow sticky note and wrote the word nervous on it in clear capital letters. She looked at the word for a moment and was astonished to find that it made the feeling a little less enormous.

In the corridor she whispered, I notice that I feel nervous, which was quite different from saying that she was nervous, and felt like holding the feeling at arm's length. When she told Yusuf about it the following Saturday, he nodded and said that some studies suggest that putting a name to a feeling can ease it. He added with a smile that his grandmother had known this long before the scientists, and had simply called it getting it off your chest.

Elise discovered that the more precise her words were, the more helpful the exercise became, and she began to widen her vocabulary beyond fine and stressed. On the next sticky note she wrote nervous, tired and, at the bottom, in smaller letters, a little hopeful, which surprised her as much as it pleased her. She had not realised that so many different weathers could blow through a single afternoon.

Feelings are not only thoughts, Yusuf told her, but also sensations, and they live in the body as surely as a hot cup lives in the hand. In a quiet room at the hospital, Elise rested a palm on her chest, closed her eyes, and asked herself where, exactly, the worry was sitting. It was a strange question, but it had an answer, and the answer arrived at once.

She found a tight band behind her breastbone, and below it, in her stomach, a hard little knot about the size of a fist. It was heavy and slightly warm, and it had a shape, which was something she had never imagined a worry could have. Observing it closely made it feel less like an enemy and more like an uncomfortable guest.

Following Yusuf's instructions, she directed her slow breaths towards the knot, as if she were gently sending warmth to a cold part of the house. After a few minutes it loosened a little, and its edges seemed less sharp, though it did not disappear entirely. That was perfectly acceptable, she decided, because the purpose was not to remove the feeling but to keep it company.

Yusuf pointed to a puddle on the path, where the last raindrops were making rings that spread, wobbled and finally subsided into stillness. Feelings behave in the same way, he said, rising and peaking and falling away of their own accord, provided that we do not keep stirring the water with our thoughts. Elise glanced at the puddle and thought that it was a rather good teacher for something that had no qualifications.

Elise told Yusuf that she was frightened of Friday's review, and that she feared her manager would find her too slow, too anxious and not strategic enough. He did not rush to reassure her or to fix anything, but simply listened, with his hands resting on his knees, until she had said everything twice. It was extraordinary how much lighter the fear felt when somebody had really heard it.

In the meeting on Friday, the familiar knot appeared in Elise's stomach as the door closed, and she quietly named it nervous and took a slow breath. Then, instead of presenting a polished and defensive account of her work, she spoke honestly about what had gone well and what had been difficult. It felt like jumping into cold water, and, like cold water, it was far less terrible once she was in.

The review was not perfect, and her manager asked some questions that she could not answer at once, but overall it went well enough. When she stepped out of the room, Elise rested a hand on her chest and felt the knot, now looser and smaller than before, and she thought that she had stayed herself in a situation that usually made her disappear. That night she bought herself a tangerine, and ate it slowly, with great ceremony.

Yusuf pushed a beach ball under the surface of the water barrel and held it there, with visible effort, until his arm began to tremble. Feelings that we push away behave in exactly the same way, he said: they demand constant energy to keep submerged, and they leap up again the moment our attention slips. It was far easier, he suggested, to let the ball float beside us and simply to get on with the digging.

When Yusuf let go, the ball erupted from the barrel with a tremendous splash, drenching them both and sending Biscuit the puppy into a frenzy of barking. Elise, wiping her face, found herself thinking of all the sadness and annoyance that she had pressed down over the years in the name of getting on with things. She had always called it being strong, and she began to wonder whether it was more like being tired.

Elise sat on the bench and allowed a quiet sadness, which she had been avoiding for weeks, to float up beside her like the ball in the barrel. She did not push it under, and she did not feed it with stories, but she kept it company and breathed, and she felt it swell, hold its shape and begin to ebb. It had been far less frightening to meet than it had been to avoid.

An angry email arrived from a senior manager who blamed Elise, in rather unforgiving language, for a mistake in the rota that had not been hers. She felt heat flood her face and her fingers fly straight to the keyboard, already composing a reply that would have been satisfying for exactly ninety seconds. Then, just in time, she remembered something that Yusuf had said to her about a beach ball and a barrel of water.

Elise stopped, laid one hand flat on the cool desk and took three slow breaths, feeling the heat in her face and the pounding of her pulse in her ears. She did not try to argue herself out of the anger, but simply gave it time to rise and pass, like a wave breaking over a rock. After the third breath, the screen looked just the same, and she was a different person looking at it.

After the breaths, Elise wrote a calm reply of two lines, stating the facts and offering to put the matter right by the end of the day. The manager replied within the hour, more politely than before, and even thanked her for her clarity, which she had not expected in a hundred years. The first draft, she knew, would have started a war, and the second had ended one before it began.

Yusuf held up a nettle in his thick gardening glove and observed that anger is rather like its sting, in that it is a signal and not an instruction. It tells you that something matters, he said, a boundary has been crossed, or a value has been bruised, and the wise response is to read the message before deciding what to do. Elise thought that this was the first time anyone had suggested that her anger might be useful.

In a drawer at home, Elise found an old note and, on impulse, wrote on it the thing that she regretted most. At twenty-two she had turned down a place on a painting course because it seemed impractical, and she had been quietly mourning that decision for thirteen years. Seeing the sentence in her own handwriting, she felt both embarrassed and a little relieved.

Yusuf asked what the regret had to teach her, and Elise thought about it for a long time before answering that she should make room, now, for the things she loved. That seemed to him a perfectly good lesson, and he suggested that she thank the regret, take the lesson and let the rest go. Elise folded the note into a small paper boat, creasing the corners with her thumbnail.

She set the little boat on the pond beneath the apple tree and watched the breeze carry it slowly out of reach, the note still folded inside. Then, for the first time in many years, she took out a pencil and began to sketch the green gate on the back of an envelope, badly and happily. It was not the painting course, but it was a beginning, and the beginning was in the present.

In the hospital canteen, Elise dropped a tray of cups with a crash that made half the room turn round, and she muttered under her breath that she was useless and stupid. Telling the story to Yusuf on Saturday, she repeated the phrases without thinking, and he put down his trowel and asked quietly whether she would ever say such things to her sister. The question landed with great force, because the honest answer was that she would not say them to a stranger.

Elise decided to try an experiment: whenever she made a mistake she would speak to herself in the tone that she used with a good friend. Standing in front of the bathroom mirror she said, rather stiffly at first, that everyone dropped things sometimes and that nobody had been hurt. It sounded ridiculous at first, and yet something in her shoulders relaxed at once, as though they had been waiting for exactly those words.

She looked into her own eyes and told the woman in the mirror that she was doing her best, which felt awkward and slightly absurd. It was also, she recognised, entirely true, and a smile arrived on her face before she had decided to produce one. Lily would have laughed at her, and she would have deserved to be laughed at, and the thought only made the smile larger.

Elise confessed that she worried that being kind to herself would make her lazy, since harshness had always been the engine that drove her forward. Yusuf looked at the row of seedlings with great affection and said that in fifty years he had never once shouted at a plant and seen it grow faster. Kindness was not the opposite of effort, he said, but the soil in which effort could keep growing.

Many nights, Elise woke at three in the morning with her heart beating faster and her thoughts racing round the track, running through tomorrow's list and the next day's after it. The dark made every problem look larger, and the quiet seemed to invite them all in to be discussed. She lay rigid under the blanket, wondering whether her mind had any intention of ever resting.

Yusuf suggested an early evening ritual, which was to write down tomorrow's tasks and worries in a notebook at about eight o'clock and then close it firmly. By turning them into ink, Elise gave her mind a safe place to leave them, like a coat check for anxieties, and she found that she trusted the notebook more than her memory. She turned off the lamp that night with the strange sense that nobody was waiting in the dark.

At three in the morning, Elise woke once more, but this time she did not wrestle with her thoughts and turned her attention to the blanket, her warm feet and the slow rise and fall of her stomach. The thoughts continued for a while, like a distant radio in another flat, and then thinned out until she could not hear them at all. It did not work perfectly every single night, but it worked often enough to give her real and growing hope.

On the nights when sleep refused to come, Elise stopped fighting it, having discovered that the struggle was more exhausting than the wakefulness. She told herself that lying quietly in the dark was still a form of rest, and that her body was benefiting even if her mind stayed awake. Oddly, with the pressure removed, sleep often crept up on her when she was no longer looking for it.

On one particularly bad day, Elise lost the form for a new night rota and, convinced that the fault was Marcus's, snapped at him in front of the whole corridor. She saw his face fall, and an unpleasant weight settled in her stomach, because she knew at once that she had been unjust. The form, as it turned out, had been under her own coffee cup the entire time.

Elise found Marcus at the end of the corridor, told him plainly that she had been unfair, and confessed to the coffee cup. He laughed, which was generous, and the weight in her stomach dissolved as if it had never been there. A bad day, she thought, did not have to run on until midnight, because there was always a next moment in which to begin again.

Elise began a new habit at work, which was to take one slow breath before beginning any task, however small. She breathed before opening her email, before dialling a number and before entering a meeting, and she found that the mornings began less like a collision and more like a gentle entry. It cost her three seconds each time and saved her, she suspected, a great deal of wasted hurry.

The single breath turned into a kind of doorway, and Elise began to pause at the threshold of each ward, office or meeting room before she stepped through. It meant that she arrived in each place, with her whole self, rather than dragging the previous room in with her, like a coat caught in a door. Her day, which had once been a single blurred rush, began to look like a sequence of separate rooms.

A bigger worry arrived with the first cool mornings of September: the hospital's winter staffing looked dangerously thin, and Elise was responsible for making the numbers work. The problem was real, and she could not simply breathe it away, but she found that it followed her home, into the shower and even into her dreams. She understood that something more organised than three slow breaths would be needed to deal with it properly.

Yusuf proposed an odd but practical idea, which was to set aside ten minutes every day for worrying, on purpose, at a fixed time. At all other times, he said, she could tell her worries politely that they had an appointment later and ask them to wait in the corridor. Elise laughed at the idea, and then, remembering how many hours she had lost to worrying by accident, she decided that it might be a bargain.

At half past six that evening, Elise set a timer for ten minutes and sat at the kitchen table with a sheet of paper divided into two columns, headed worries and next steps. She wrote down everything that frightened her about the winter, and beside each item she wrote the smallest action that she could take. When the timer rang, she closed the notebook and was amazed that it had not taken longer.

The next day, in the supermarket, a worry about the weekend rota leapt into Elise's mind and demanded immediate attention, and she told it politely that worry time was at half past six. To her amazement it went, grumbling, and she was able to carry on choosing apples without a shadow across her face. The postponement felt rather like telling a persistent salesman to call back after supper.

Some of her worries, she found, had no next step at all, because they depended entirely on things beyond her power, such as the weather, the flu season and other people's decisions. Beside these she wrote, in firm capitals, nothing to do now, and she was surprised by how restful the phrase turned out to be. It was a kind of permission, issued by herself, to stop carrying what could not be carried.

After a week of daily appointments, Elise looked at her list and saw that it had grown noticeably shorter, as though it had been sitting in a warm room. Some worries had been solved by the steps she had taken, and others had simply expired, like old tickets, without ever being used. The remaining ones were smaller, clearer and far easier to manage, and she felt a surge of gratitude towards the little timer.

On Saturday morning, straight from her night shift and still in her blue uniform, Priya pushed open the green gate and stood blinking in the morning light. She looked exhausted and a little wary, like a cat entering a new house, but Yusuf greeted her as if she were a long-awaited guest and placed a trowel in her hand. Elise watched her and remembered how it had felt to stand in exactly that spot.

Yusuf asked Priya to close her eyes and press her hands into the soil, and she obeyed with the weary obedience of someone who had been told to do stranger things at four in the morning. Within a minute her shoulders had lowered by what seemed like several inches, and a small, astonished smile appeared on her face. Watching her, Elise saw the garden as though for the first time, and understood that it was no longer only hers.

One morning, the sun came through Elise's kitchen window and laid a bright, trembling shape of light across the wall. She stopped with the kettle in her hand and watched it for a full minute, as it slid, bent over the edge of a shelf and turned the dust in the air into gold. She had lived in that kitchen for six years without ever noticing that it did this.

Elise began a game on her walk to work, in which she had to find one beautiful thing each morning, however small or humble. She discovered a spider's web strung with dew like a necklace, a plume of steam curling from a bakery vent, and a tiny red shoe set carefully on a wall by someone who hoped its owner would return. The city, she saw, was full of tiny private galleries that were open to anybody who cared to look at them.

Yusuf held a green bean pod up against the sun, and its seams glowed like the veins of a leaf. Beauty is not rare, he told her, because it is attention that is scarce, and a garden is nothing more than ordinary things looked at very carefully for a very long time. The sentence stayed with her all week, as a pebble stays in a shoe.

Yusuf suggested a habit that he had practised for years, which was to write down three good things at the end of each day. Some studies suggest that noting a few good things can lift mood a little, he said, though he preferred to think of it as keeping a very small diary of thanks. Elise bought a small green notebook on the way home and wrote the date on the first page.

On the first evening, Elise sat with her pen poised and a blank mind, convinced that the day had contained nothing worth recording. Slowly, the small things surfaced: the warm toast at breakfast, Priya's smile across the canteen and a ladybird that had walked across her sleeve during lunch. By the time she had written them down, the day itself looked different, as if somebody had changed the lighting.

After two weeks of writing in the little green book, Elise found that she had begun to collect good things as they happened, instead of at the end of the day. When a colleague laughed at one of her jokes or the afternoon light fell on the carpet, she would think, privately and with great satisfaction, that is one. Her attention had been quietly retrained to look for what was working, as well as what was going wrong.

Elise admitted to Yusuf that the little notebook did not cure her bad days, and that on some evenings the three good things seemed laughably small. He agreed without any hurt pride, and said that the habit was like adding a small weight to the lighter side of a scale, which did not remove the other side but did change the balance. It was not magic, he said with a shrug, only a little patient arithmetic that added up slowly over many weeks.

On one Saturday afternoon in the garden, Elise glanced at the old clock by the shed and could hardly believe that only two hours had passed since lunch. She had weeded, talked, drunk tea, watched a wasp and sat in the sun, and the afternoon felt as rich and roomy as a whole day. When she gave her full attention to a moment, it seemed, the moment stretched to hold it.

At work, by contrast, whole afternoons evaporated, leaving only a faint memory of screens, a headache and a sense of vague guilt. Elise began to see the difference between being busy and being full, because the first used up the hours and the second filled them. She had spent years collecting busyness and wondering why it never made her feel rich.

Attention, Yusuf told her as they picked the first large basket of beans, is the way a person actually spends his days, since a life is made of whatever one has noticed. They worked their way along the rows in the late sun, snapping each pod from its stem and dropping it into the basket with a small, satisfying sound. Elise thought that it was the most expensive and the cheapest thing that she owned, and she was determined to spend it better.

Yusuf asked Elise to sit on the bench for five minutes and do absolutely nothing, a request that she found surprisingly alarming. No phone, no notebook, no practice, he said, only sitting, while the bees went about their work among the lavender. It sounded easy, and she suspected that it would be the hardest thing he had yet asked of her.

After one minute, a wave of guilt rose in her, as if she had been caught stealing time from an employer who happened to be herself. Her hand crept towards her pocket and the phone inside it, and in the end she was obliged to sit on both hands like a naughty schoolgirl. Yusuf, who appeared to be fast asleep beside her in the sunshine, smiled without even opening his eyes.

Gradually Elise discovered that resting, like walking or cooking, was a skill that could be learned and not merely an absence of activity. She noticed the weight of her shoulders, the slow drone of the bees and the warmth on her face, and the minutes softened and spread out like butter on warm bread. When Yusuf finally said that the five minutes were over, she was genuinely disappointed, and asked him whether she could have another five.

Rest, Yusuf told her, is not a reward that one earns by finishing the work, but an essential part of the work itself, like the quiet between the notes in a piece of music. He pointed to a patch of bare soil that he would leave fallow over the winter, and said that the ground, too, needed its seasons of doing nothing. Elise wrote it in the little green book as one of the three good things, though it was far too large to fit in a line.

One Saturday, Yusuf led her to a small wood on the edge of the city, where the path was soft with fallen leaves and the tall trees stood on either side like patient guards. He walked slowly, stopping now and then to look at a fungus or to listen to a woodpecker, and Elise found that she did the same. She had not known that a place so quiet existed within half an hour of her desk.

Some studies suggest that spending time among plants and trees can help people to feel calmer, Yusuf remarked, though he said that he had never needed a study to tell him so. Elise did not need one either, since she could feel her breathing deepen, her shoulders loosen and the clutter in her head begin to settle like mud in a pond. The green all around her seemed to ask for nothing, and to expect nothing, and to be perfectly content with that arrangement.

In the heart of the wood they came upon an enormous oak, wide enough that three people could not have circled it with their arms, and Yusuf rested his palm against its bark. Elise did the same, feeling the ridges under her hand, and had a moment of dizzying smallness in which her deadlines seemed to be of no consequence. She felt strangely, deeply fine, as if she had been reminded of a fact that she had forgotten.

On a rainy evening at home, Elise sat by the window watching the lights of a distant train, and she caught herself in a very familiar thought. When the winter staffing plan was finished, she told herself, then she would be able to relax and be happy. It was the same sentence that she had said about the last project, and the one before that, and she suddenly saw the shape of the trap.

Yusuf confessed that for years he too had lived by the sentence when the garden is finished, then I will rest, and that he had said it every spring without ever noticing the joke. A garden is never finished, he said, and neither is a working life, and the happiness that was waiting at the end of a task was usually the same happiness that was available at the beginning. Elise laughed aloud with relief, because the sentence sounded exactly like something that she herself might have said last week.

That evening, Elise wrote four words on a yellow sticky note and pressed it onto the door of her fridge: not when, but now. She had no illusions that it would transform her life, but she liked how it made her stop for a second each time she reached for the milk. Perhaps happiness was not a destination at the end of the timetable, she thought, but a station that the train kept passing through.

After dinner, Elise ran a bowl of hot water, added a squirt of soap and began to wash the dishes without any music or podcast. The water was warm around her wrists, the bubbles shone with tiny rainbows, and the blue bowl slid smoothly through her fingers like a pebble in a stream. It occurred to her that she had always thought of this as a chore.

She felt the changing heat of the water, smelled the lemon in the soap, and watched each plate gleam as it emerged from the suds. Ten minutes passed in a kind of contented trance, and when she had finished the last glass, the kitchen was clean and her mind was almost equally so. She had not expected to find a break from the day in a sink of dirty plates.

Elise resolved to choose one ordinary task each day and perform it with her whole attention, and on Tuesday she chose folding the laundry. The towels were warm from the dryer and smelled of clean cotton, and she smoothed each one with her palms, matching the corners with a precision that gave her unexpected pleasure. Tasks that she had always rushed through turned out to have a texture of their own, and a rhythm that was almost musical.

One grey morning the bus was fifteen minutes late, and Elise stood at the stop with her phone deliberately buried in the bottom of her bag. She felt the old itch to escape from the emptiness, to fill the gap with scrolling, and she let it itch without scratching. Boredom, she was beginning to suspect, was less an enemy than a door that she had never been willing to open.

A pigeon strutted along the pavement in front of her with its head bobbing, and as it passed through a shaft of light, its neck flashed green and violet like oil on water. She watched it for several minutes, amused by its pompous walk and the earnest way that it investigated a crumb. She wondered how long it had been since she had really looked at a pigeon, and realised that the answer was never.

After a few minutes of quiet looking, an idea slid into Elise's mind without being invited, a fresh way of arranging the weekend shifts that would give every nurse a free Sunday once a month. She found a pen in her bag and wrote the key points on her hand, laughing at herself. The solution had been waiting for a spare minute, and she had never given it one.

At lunchtime, Marcus asked Elise shyly whether she would mind sitting with him on a bench in the park, and she could tell at once that something was weighing on him. He unwrapped his sandwich without eating it, and began to speak about his father, who was growing frail and forgetful and who lived alone two hundred miles away. Elise felt the old urge to find a quick solution rise within her, and she wondered whether she would be able to resist it.

Elise let the urge to fix things float past, as she had learned to do with the beach ball, and she turned her whole body towards Marcus. She offered no advice and no stories about her own father, but asked a single gentle question, which was what he was most afraid of. He thought for a long moment and then answered, and his voice, which had been tight, began to unwind.

When Marcus had finished, he thanked her warmly and said that very few people ever simply listened, and that he felt lighter than he had in months. Elise, who had said hardly anything, saw that she had given him something real, and that it had cost her nothing but her attention. Giving someone one's full attention, she thought, might be the best gift that one had to offer.

Elise and Marcus walked back from the park together in the thin autumn sunshine, and she thought about how many chances she had every day to give someone her attention. In corridors, lifts, canteens and kitchens, there were people who would have been quietly glad to be heard, and she had walked past most of them. It was a gift that required no wrapping and no budget, and it was always in stock.

On a quiet morning in the first week of autumn, Elise noticed that Yusuf was unusually still, with one hand resting on the back of the bench. She had sat on that bench dozens of times, and she realised with a small shock that she had never read the small brass plaque screwed to its frame. It said, in simple capital letters, for Aylin, and underneath was a date from some years before.

Elise did not ask, but Yusuf began to speak, quietly and without hurry, about Aylin, who had been his wife for forty-one years and who had died some years earlier. They had built the bench together one spring, he said, from planks that Aylin had insisted on sanding herself, and she had loved to sit beneath the apple tree and tell him that the carrots were crooked. His eyes were bright, and his voice did not shake at all, though Elise could see how much the words cost him.

After Aylin died, Yusuf told her, he could not bear to sit at home among her coats and her cups, and so he walked to the garden every morning and pushed his hands into the earth. It did not take his grief away, and he had never expected that it would, but it gave his grief somewhere to stand and his hands something to do. The soil asked nothing of him, as a faithful friend might, except that he should be there and keep it company.

Presence does not remove pain, Yusuf said, and anyone who promised that it did was selling something, but it allowed a person to meet the pain with kindness instead of panic. Elise found that her eyes had filled, though she could not have said exactly why, and Yusuf handed her an old cotton handkerchief that smelled faintly of mint. They sat for a long time without speaking, and it was one of the most honest conversations of her life.

Yusuf added, quite firmly, that the garden had not been the only thing to help him, and that in the worst months he had also visited a counsellor every week. Heavy or lasting worry, or a low mood that will not lift, is a good reason to talk to a doctor or counsellor, he said, and there is no shame in it whatever. He left a small folded leaflet on the bench between them, as a gardener leaves a seed packet.

A few days later, Priya admitted to Elise in a quiet corner of the hospital that she had been feeling low for months, long after the night shifts had stopped explaining it. Elise listened without interrupting and then, with great gentleness, repeated what Yusuf had said about doctors and counsellors, and handed over the leaflet that he had given her. She did not pretend to be an expert and offered no diagnosis, only the encouragement of a friend, and Priya booked an appointment with her doctor for the following Wednesday, right there on the bench.

The meeting about winter staffing had a reputation for being difficult, with tired managers, anxious ward leaders and an unwelcome budget on the table. Elise paused at the door, took one slow breath and felt her feet on the floor, and then stepped in with a steadiness that she would not have recognised a year earlier. She chose a seat, set down her folder and looked around the table at everyone's faces.

Instead of rehearsing her answers while others spoke, as she would once have done, Elise listened to each person with her full attention. Beneath the arguments about budgets and rotas she heard a single, repeated concern, which was that nobody wanted to leave the night wards short of experienced staff. It was exactly what Priya had described to her on the park bench, and the realisation struck her like a clear bell.

When her turn came, Elise spoke calmly and plainly, naming the real problem first and then sketching a plan that protected the night wards and shared the weekend shifts more fairly. There was a short silence, then a murmur of agreement, and a senior nurse said that it was the first sensible suggestion she had heard all week. Across the table, Marcus caught her eye and smiled, as though they shared a pleasant secret.

At home, Elise discovered a daily anchor in the most ordinary of objects, which was the kettle. Every time she switched it on, she stood still beside it, closed her eyes and breathed, listening as the water began to murmur, rumble and finally roar. It took about two minutes, it needed no equipment, and it had become the most dependable part of her day.

On a golden October morning, Elise knelt at the carrot bed and pulled the first carrot from the earth, where it had been working in the dark for months. It was crooked, orange and slightly forked, and it was the most beautiful vegetable she had ever seen. The basket beside her was already full of beans and bright leaves, and the garden looked tired and generous, like a host at the end of a party.

Yusuf held a harvest supper under the apple tree, at a long table made of three smaller ones and lit with candles in jam jars. Nora and Tomas came with Lily, Priya arrived looking rested and a little shy, Marcus brought a cake, and Rosa, headphones round her neck, carried the soup. It was made from the garden's own beans and carrots, and Elise noticed that everyone ate it slowly.

Looking along the candlelit table, Elise thought of the woman who had stared at her phone on a spring morning and carried on three stops past her destination. That woman had lived mostly in the future, with a flicker of the past, and had barely met a single person on the way. The woman at the table was the same one, and yet she felt entirely different.

The next morning, Elise was weeding when her mind drifted off to a spreadsheet, a birthday and a conversation that she was planning for Tuesday, and she knocked her trowel clean out of her hand. It landed on a flowerpot with a clang that made Biscuit bark and Yusuf look up, and Elise burst out laughing. The mind still wandered, even after a season of practice, and she found that she no longer minded in the slightest.

The aim was never a perfectly quiet mind, Yusuf told her, any more than the aim of the sea was to be flat. What mattered was the gentle return, repeated again and again, with a smile and without scolding, until it became as natural as breathing in after breathing out. A mind that wandered and came home, he said, was a mind in excellent health.

Each morning now, before she looked at her phone, Elise wrote a single word on a small white card beside her cup of tea, such as gentle, listen or curious. It was an intention, not a goal, and it pointed her gently towards the day without dragging her out of the present. The word was not a promise, she thought, but a direction, like a compass needle that she could consult whenever she lost her way.

On a damp Sunday morning, Elise brought Lily to the garden, and the two of them crouched beside a snail on a wet leaf, their noses almost touching the glistening trail. The snail extended its soft horns, withdrew them, thought about it, and extended them again. Lily was perfectly motionless, her mouth slightly open, in a state of attention that Elise had spent a whole season trying to learn.

Lily put a finger to her lips and whispered that Aunty Elise must stop talking and listen, because the snail was on its way to work and might be late. Elise listened, and heard the rustle of a leaf, the drip of rain and, if she was honest, nothing whatever from the snail. Children, she thought, were born knowing what she had taken months to learn, and the gift was to remember it.

Before the first frost, Yusuf pressed his old trowel into Elise's hands, its wooden handle polished smooth by decades of use. His knees, he said with a grin, now preferred a warm fire in winter, and he would be in the shed with his tea and his opinions, supervising. The garden was hers to look after, and the best way to look after it, he said, was to be there.

Here is the whole lesson in a few lines: your life happens in this moment, so notice where your mind has gone and bring it gently home through your senses, your breath and your hands. Do one thing at a time, treat your feelings with curiosity, and be as kind to yourself as you would be to a friend. Then begin again, as often as necessary, because the present moment always returns and always offers a new start.
